intro.html: Honesty comes in flavors. A candid friend admits mistakes; a frank one tells you what you would rather not hear; a sincere one means every word. Dishonesty has flavors too: the devious person sneaks around the rules, the duplicitous one plays both sides, and the disingenuous one pretends to be more innocent than he is.

Honest: candid (open), frank (blunt), sincere (meant), forthright (speaks up directly), integrity (honesty all the way through), guileless (innocent, no tricks). Dishonest: deceitful (lying), devious (sneaky), duplicitous (two-faced), disingenuous (falsely innocent).

words.def: open and honest in what one says
words.ex: In a {candid} interview, the coach admitted the team had played badly.
words.ctx: Rather than make excuses, Pip was {candid}: he told his mother exactly how the vase had broken and offered to pay for a new one from his allowance.
words.etym: From Latin candidus, “white, pure,” related to candle: a candid answer has nothing hidden in the shadows.
words.note: A candid photo is an unposed one, taken without the subject getting ready.

mn.cue: CAN + DID: I CAN tell what I DID
mn.text: “I did it. I broke the vase,” says Pip, before anyone even asks. He can tell what he did: he is {candid}.

cast.say: I did it. I broke the vase.

scene.alt: A boy openly admits to his surprised mother that he broke the vase.

words.def: direct and honest, even when it is uncomfortable
words.ex: Dad was {frank} with us: the car needed repairs, and the trip would have to wait.
words.ctx: Most guests politely praised the soup, but Grandma was {frank}: she said it needed salt, pepper and about an hour more on the stove.
words.etym: From Old French franc, “free”: a frank speaker feels free to say what she thinks.

mn.text: Nana Lou tastes the soup and gives it to you straight as a plank: “Needs salt. Lots of salt.” No sugarcoating: she is {frank}.

scene.alt: A grandmother tastes the cook’s soup and bluntly says it needs salt.

words.def: meaning what one says; free of pretense
words.ex: Her apology was {sincere}; she had tears in her eyes.
words.ctx: Unlike the salesman’s rehearsed compliments, the boy’s thank-you note was {sincere}: he had written it himself, misspellings and all, because he loved the gift.

mn.cue: sin-SEER: you can SEE he means it
mn.text: Theo hands Mom a crumpled crayon card that says “I LUV U,” and she can see he means every word. His card is {sincere}.

labels.text: sin-SEER: you SEE he means it

scene.alt: A toddler hands his kneeling mother a homemade card, and she is moved.

words.def: direct and outspoken; saying plainly what one thinks
words.ex: The {forthright} referee explained exactly why the goal did not count.
words.ctx: Instead of hinting that the budget was a problem, the treasurer was {forthright}: she stood up at the meeting and said the club would run out of money by June.
words.etym: From Old English forthriht, “straight forward”: forth (forward) + riht (straight).

mn.cue: FORTH-RIGHT: steps FORTH, says it RIGHT
mn.text: When Rex cuts into the ticket line, Maya steps forth and says it right out: “That’s not fair. The line starts back there.” She is {forthright}.

scene.alt: A teen girl steps forward and tells a line-cutter plainly to go to the back.

words.def: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles
words.ex: A person of {integrity} keeps a promise even when no one would ever find out.
words.ctx: When the cashier handed her twenty dollars too much in change, Rosa showed her {integrity}: she walked back across the parking lot to return it.
words.etym: From Latin integritas, “wholeness,” from integer, whole: the same word as the integer of math.

mn.text: Like a whole number, Rosa is honest all the way through: she finds a wallet full of cash and returns every dollar to its owner. She has {integrity}.

scene.alt: A teenager returns a lost wallet to its delighted owner on a city street.

words.def: trying to make others believe what is false
words.ex: The {deceitful} player pretended to be hurt so the referee would call a foul.
words.ctx: The ad looked friendly, but it was {deceitful}: tiny print at the bottom revealed that the “free” game cost ten dollars a month.
words.etym: From deceit, Old French deceite, from Latin decipere, “to catch, to trap.”

mn.cue: de-SEE-tful: you SEE what isn’t there
mn.text: Rex paints a plain rock gold and tells the tourists it is pirate treasure. Making people see what isn’t there is {deceitful}.

scene.alt: A sneaky man in a pirate hat paints a rock gold and claims it is real treasure.

words.def: sly and tricky in getting one’s way
words.ex: The cat came up with a {devious} plan to reach the fish tank.
words.ctx: Rather than ask for a later bedtime, the {devious} twins quietly set every clock in the house back an hour.
words.etym: From Latin devius, “off the road”: de (away from) + via (way).

mn.text: Instead of asking for a later bedtime, Pip and Ivy take the sneaky road: they tiptoe in and turn the clock back an hour. That trick is {devious}.

scene.alt: Two sneaky kids tiptoe to the bedroom clock and turn it back.

words.def: two-faced; saying one thing and doing another
words.ex: The {duplicitous} spy smiled at both sides while secretly working for neither.
words.ctx: The knight seemed loyal to the king, but he was {duplicitous}: by day he guarded the castle, and by night he sent messages to the king’s enemies.
words.etym: From duplicity, Latin duplicitas, “doubleness,” from duplex, double.

mn.text: Rex smiles at the queen, “I’m your loyal knight!”, then turns around and whispers plans to the dragon. Two faces, like a duplicate: he is {duplicitous}.

scene.alt: The same knight appears twice: bowing loyally to the queen, and whispering plans to a dragon.

words.def: insincere; pretending to be more innocent or less informed than one is
words.ex: It was {disingenuous} of Dev to ask “What cookies?” with chocolate on his chin.
words.ctx: The company’s claim that it had “no idea” its toys were breaking was {disingenuous}; its own engineers had warned about the problem a year earlier.
words.etym: From dis (not) + ingenuous, “innocent, frank,” from Latin ingenuus, “freeborn, noble.”
words.note: Disingenuous is not the opposite of ingenious (clever); it is the opposite of ingenuous (innocent, frank).

mn.text: “What cookies?” asks Dev, wide-eyed, with chocolate all over his chin and an empty jar behind him. Pretending to be innocent like that is {disingenuous}.

scene.alt: A boy with crumbs on his face shrugs innocently beside an empty cookie jar while his mother frowns.

words.def: innocent and without tricks; open and honest
words.ex: The puppy’s {guileless} eyes made it impossible to stay angry.
words.ctx: Unlike the sly older players, the new girl was {guileless}: she told everyone her strategy before the game and was surprised when they used it against her.

mn.text: Theo plays cards holding his hand face out so everyone can see it: no tricks, no secrets, no bluffing. He is {guileless}.

scene.alt: A toddler happily shows everyone his cards while his grandfather laughs.

head: honest word
what it adds
rows: means what is said; no pretending
no tricks at all, sometimes too trusting

after.html: Three look-alikes: ingenious means clever; ingenuous means innocent and frank; disingenuous means falsely innocent. A disingenuous person pretends to be ingenuous.

items.q: Which word means pretending to be innocent or sincere?
items.why: Disingenuous: dis (not) + ingenuous (innocent, frank). Ingenious means clever, which is a different word.

items.q: True or false: a candid photo is one where everyone poses and smiles.
items.why: False. A candid photo is unposed, taken naturally. Candid means open and honest.

items.q: The spy promised loyalty to both kingdoms and betrayed them both. He was…
items.why: Playing both sides while lying to each is duplicitous: two-faced.

choices: admitting a mistake that no one else noticed
winning a game by bending the rules
telling a friend only what she wants to hear
items.why: Integrity is honesty and strong principles even when no one is watching.
